newsitem.title: USA: Documents point to GOP fund raising in White House.
newsitem.headline: Documents point to GOP fund raising in White House.

text.p: Republican presidents George Bush and Ronald Reagan hosted campaign donors at the White House, and a 1995 Republican dinner promised those who gave $45,000 a lunch date with House Speaker Newt Gingrich, according to network reports.

The reports follow allegations of improper and illegal fund raising by the Democratic Party and the Clinton White House during the 1996 presidential campaign, including controversial sleepovers at the White House and small coffee meetings with President Clinton and other senior White House officials.
But the new documents appear to show such practices were also used by Republicans.
ABC cited an invitation to the White House sent to donors by Reagan's fund raisers in 1988, which said, "I hope you will accept the invitation ... and make your $2,500 contribution right away."
Bush entertained big donors, known as "Eagles", 18 times in the White House, ABC said.
ABC and CBS News both reported about a 1995 GOP fund-raising dinner which appeared to sell access to senior officials, including Gingrich and then-Senate Majority Leader Bob Dole.
For a $15,000 contribution, donors got the dinner and breakfast with Dole in the Senate Caucus Room, plus briefings with key Republican committee chairmen.
For $45,000, they got all that and lunch with Gingrich in the Great Hall of the Library of Congress, the networks said.
Donors who gave $100,000 additionally were invited to a private reception after the dinner, attended by all the major players.
ABC quoted former Bush counsel Boyden Gray as saying the White House was not used as a fund-raising vehicle when Reagan and Bush were in office.
Republicans have been pressing Attorney General Janet Reno to seek appointment of an independent counsel to investigate the Democratic fund-raising practices.

Their case was bolstered after last week's disclosures that Vice President Al Gore solicited campaign funds by telephone from his White House office and that Maggie Williams, Hillary Rodham Clinton's top aide, accepted a $50,000 political donation from a Taiwanese-American entrepreneur.
A Justice Department task force is already investigating the matter.

Democratic lawmakers including Representative Henry Waxman of California have insisted that Republicans in the White House and Congress have long followed similar practices as those now being questioned at the White House.

Former Clinton adviser Dick Morris, who previously worked for Republican lawmakers, last week said at least six Republicans still serving on Capitol Hill asked donors for contributions in telephone conversations while he was present in their congressional offices.
It is illegal to solicit campaign contributions in federal offices.
CBS cited a fund-raising letter for Sen. Christopher Bond, a Missouri Republican, in which he invites donors to contact him in his Senate office.
Bond said his Senate telephone number was listed by mistake and he never used his office to raise money.
